passage:
It was the week of the half-yearly exams, and the school bus came at 6:40. Kishore had been awake till two every night, half revising, half watching cricket clips under the blanket.
By Wednesday, everything felt wrong. He read the same chemistry line five times. When his sister Gopika asked to borrow his calculator, he snapped, "Can't you get your own for once?" and then felt terrible. At lunch he nearly cried because the canteen had run out of samosas.
"What's wrong with me?" he muttered. "I'm becoming a horrible person."
Gopika, still annoyed, looked at the dark rings under his eyes. "You're not horrible. You're just not sleeping. You were exactly like this last year."
That night, grudgingly, he put the phone in the kitchen and slept at ten-thirty. Thursday wasn't perfect. But the chemistry made sense, and he laughed at Gopika's joke at breakfast.

qa.q: What time did the school bus come?
qa.a: The school bus came at 6:40.

qa.q: What was Kishore worried about when he muttered "What's wrong with me?"
qa.a: Kishore felt ashamed and frightened that his snapping and near-tears meant he was becoming a horrible person.

qa.q: What small change helped Kishore, and why?
qa.a: Putting his phone in the kitchen and sleeping at ten-thirty, because his irritability and fog came from lost sleep, not his character.

qa.q: How did Gopika see Kishore's mood that week?
qa.a: Gopika was annoyed at first but understood it as tiredness rather than him being horrible, since she'd seen it the year before.

grounding: A teenager staying up late becomes irritable, foggy and reactive, mistaking sleep debt for a personality flaw.

passage:
Class teacher's note, board exam week
I've been watching two students this week. Bidisha has been studying till three every night; today she came in pale, forgot a formula she knew well, and cried in the corridor.
Afreen is just as worried about the exams, and says so. But she has kept a plan: lights off by eleven, a twenty-minute walk with her mother after dinner, and proper meals, not biscuits at her desk. This morning she told me, "If I skip sleep, I forget everything I learned anyway."
In today's revision test, Afreen recalled the long answers clearly. Bidisha, usually the stronger student, went blank on two.
What I did next: I spoke to Bidisha privately and gently, suggested she try Afreen's routine for the rest of the week, and I'll check in with her on Friday. I'll also share a short note on rest with all parents.

qa.q: What time does Afreen turn off her lights?
qa.a: Afreen turns her lights off by eleven.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling about the exams?
qa.a: Afreen felt just as worried as others about the exams, but calm enough to trust her routine.

qa.q: What would you advise a student in Bidisha's place?
qa.a: Keep sleep, a short walk and proper meals on schedule, as Afreen does, since tired minds forget what they already know.

qa.q: How was Bidisha affected by studying till three?
qa.a: Bidisha felt exhausted and upset, forgetting a formula she knew and going blank in the test despite being a strong student.

grounding: An adult's note shows a wise student keeping sleep, a walk and meals in exam season, recalling better than one who crams.

passage:
I'm Irawati, Ira's flatmate, and I've watched her do something strange for a year now.
Every Saturday her phone goes into a drawer at ten in the morning and stays there till dinner. She doesn't check work messages; her team knows to call her sister in an emergency. She cooks a slow breakfast, reads on the balcony, walks to the lake, naps without an alarm.
At first I thought she was being lazy, or antisocial. We work at similar firms, and I was working Saturdays, proud of it.
Then last winter I got sick, properly run down, for two weeks. Ira didn't. When I asked her about it, she shrugged and said, "I don't wait to crash before I rest."
I don't know everything she feels on those Saturdays. But on Mondays she looks awake. Now my phone goes in a drawer on Sundays.

qa.q: Where does Ira put her phone on Saturdays?
qa.a: Her phone goes into a drawer at ten in the morning and stays there till dinner.

qa.q: What did Irawati first think of Ira's Saturdays, and how did that change?
qa.a: Irawati first felt a little superior, thinking Ira lazy, but after getting run down Irawati felt humbled and curious enough to copy the habit.

qa.q: Why does Ira's weekly rest work?
qa.a: Ira rests regularly before she crashes, with a real day off and no messages, which prevents burnout rather than repairing it.

qa.q: What would change if Ira only rested after exhaustion?
qa.a: Ira might end up run down like Irawati last winter, needing weeks to recover instead of staying fresh each Monday.

grounding: An observer watches a young worker build regular weekly rest into life, as prevention rather than a reward after collapse.

passage:
Sunday
Today cousin Kiran came over and wanted me to play hide and seek with all the neighbourhood kids. I said I was reading. Kiran said, "You're so boring! Are you sad or something?"
I'm NOT sad. I was reading my detective book in my corner behind the almirah, with a pillow and a guava. It was the best part, where the dog finds the key.
Mummy made me go out anyway. I played for ten minutes and kept thinking about the key. It felt like someone had grabbed my book out of my hands.
When they went home, I went back to my corner. The key was in the well! I knew it!
I like being alone sometimes. It's not a sad thing. It's a quiet thing.
Aditi

qa.q: Where does Aditi read?
qa.a: Aditi reads in a corner behind the almirah, with a pillow and a guava.

qa.q: How did Aditi feel when made to go out and play?
qa.a: Aditi felt annoyed and interrupted, as if someone had grabbed the book away.

qa.q: How could Mummy handle this next time?
qa.a: Mummy could let Aditi finish the chapter first, or ask whether Aditi wants company, instead of forcing Aditi to join in.

qa.q: How does Kiran see Aditi's reading alone?
qa.a: Kiran sees it as boring or a sign of sadness, not understanding that Aditi feels content alone.

grounding: A child happily reads alone and feels content, and being pushed to socialise feels like an intrusion.

"Pranav, you're worried about that quiet boy in your class? Let old Tarun Sir tell you something.
"Thirty years ago I had a student called Bablu. Ten years old. At every break he sat under the gulmohar tree with a notebook while the others played. I was sure something was wrong. I pushed him into the cricket team, into the drama club, into group projects. He did them all. He looked miserable in every one.
"Finally I asked him, quietly, 'Is anything troubling you at home or with the boys?' I watched his face carefully. He said, 'No, Sir. I just like thinking alone.'
"I checked with his mother. Everything was fine. So I let him be.
"That notebook was full of bird drawings. Today he's a wildlife photographer, Pranav. Check for real trouble, yes. But some children are simply built for the tree.

qa.q: What was Bablu's notebook full of?
qa.a: That notebook was full of bird drawings.

qa.q: What was young Tarun Sir feeling when he saw Bablu alone at every break?
qa.a: Young Tarun Sir felt worried and sure something was wrong, which is why he kept pushing Bablu into groups.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Tarun Sir quietly asked about real trouble and checked with Bablu's mother; finding none, he let Bablu be, respecting his temperament.

qa.q: How did Bablu experience being pushed into groups?
qa.a: Bablu felt miserable in every group activity, because he simply enjoyed thinking alone.

grounding: An elder recalls worrying about a quiet child and pushing him into groups, then checking for distress and accepting his temperament.

passage:
I'm Chetan, and last winter I spent most evenings in my room with the door closed. Mum thought I was studying. My friend Yogesh thought I was busy. I told everyone I liked being alone.
Some nights that was true. I'd draw, listen to music, and feel full, like I was filling up a tank.
Other nights, I'd sit on the bed and watch the group chat, everyone laughing about some plan I wasn't in, and something in my chest ached. I'd want to text Yogesh and then not. The door was the same door. What was behind it wasn't.
Honestly, I didn't always know which kind of night it was until it was over.
One of the aching nights, Yogesh texted: "cycling tomorrow?" I nearly said "busy". I said "yes". We rode for an hour and I laughed more than I had in weeks.
Now I ask myself: am I recharging, or am I hiding?

qa.q: Who texted Chetan about cycling?
qa.a: Yogesh texted: "cycling tomorrow?"

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling on the aching nights?
qa.a: Chetan felt lonely and left out, watching the group chat laugh about plans that left Chetan out, and aching to reach out.

qa.q: What question could help Chetan, or anyone, on a closed-door night?
qa.a: Asking "Am I recharging, or am I hiding?" helps tell whether time alone is filling them up or cutting them off.

qa.q: How might Yogesh have seen Chetan's closed door?
qa.a: Yogesh thought Chetan was just busy, not knowing that some nights Chetan was lonely and hoping for a message.

grounding: A teenager alone in a closed room is sometimes recharging and sometimes aching for connection, and isn't always sure which.

passage:
Friday night
Came home from school and shut my door. Didn't want anyone. I'm writing my own songs now, in this notebook, and they're mine, not for anyone to read yet.
Mummy knocked once. I thought, here we go: "What are you doing? Who are you talking to? Open the door." Bua does that to my cousin, reads her messages and everything.
But Mummy just said through the door, "Tenzin, there's momos in the kitchen. I'll be on the balcony if you want company." Then she went away.
I stayed in my room another hour and finished the second verse. Then I went out to the balcony and sat with her. We didn't talk much. At some point I told her I was writing songs. She said, "I'd love to hear one someday. Only when you want."
Kalyani Tamang, my mummy, is the best.

qa.q: What is Tenzin writing in the notebook?
qa.a: Tenzin is writing songs in the notebook.

qa.q: What did Tenzin expect when Mummy knocked?
qa.a: Tenzin felt wary and defensive, expecting questions and pressure to open the door, like Bua does with the cousin.

qa.q: Why did Mummy's approach build trust?
qa.a: She respected the closed door, offered food and her company without conditions, and didn't demand to hear the songs.

qa.q: What might Kalyani have felt sitting on the balcony that evening?
qa.a: Kalyani likely felt patient and quietly hopeful, and touched when Tenzin came out and shared about the songs.

grounding: A teenager who shuts the door is building an inner life, and a parent who respects solitude while staying available keeps trust.

passage:
I'm Akash, and I share an office pod with Minakshi at the consulting firm. For months she was like the rest of us: answering emails at dinner, on calls at midnight.
Then, one Monday in March, she started arriving thirty minutes late, having told the team in advance. "I walk to the lake at seven, without my phone," she said. "It's on my calendar as a meeting."
I thought it was a waste. We had so much to do.
But I noticed things. She made decisions faster. When the client changed the brief, she didn't panic; she said, "I thought about this on the walk," and had a plan. In our Thursday review she was the one who spotted the flaw in the budget model.
I don't know what goes on in her head by the lake. But she comes back sorted.
Last week I asked if I could join her. She said, "Walk your own lake, Akash. That's the point."

qa.q: What time does Minakshi walk to the lake?
qa.a: She walks to the lake at seven, without her phone.

qa.q: What was Akash thinking when Minakshi started her walks?
qa.a: Akash felt doubtful and a little impatient, thinking the walk was a waste when there was so much work.

qa.q: Why does Minakshi's morning walk help her work?
qa.a: Scheduled quiet time without a device gives her space to sort her thoughts, so she decides faster and stays calm when plans change.

qa.q: Why did Minakshi tell Akash, "Walk your own lake"?
qa.a: Minakshi values the solitude itself, so company would spoil it; she wants Akash to find a separate quiet time.

grounding: An observer sees a young professional schedule device-free solitude and notices it sorts her thoughts and sharpens decisions.

passage:
In the Bengaluru office canteen, Trisha realised it had been six weeks since Deepika had come for Friday dinner. First it was "tired". Then "work". Then just a thumbs-up and no reply. Her messages, once long and full of jokes, were now one word.
Trisha remembered Deepika saying, months ago, that she liked her own company. That was true. But this felt different, like a slow fading.
She didn't want to push or make a big scene. So she texted: "No plan, no pressure. I'm going to buy flowers at the market on Sunday morning. Want to walk with me? Even ten minutes."
No reply that day. Trisha felt the urge to send a second, worried message, and didn't.
Sunday morning, 8:10: "ok. ten minutes."
They walked for an hour. Deepika said very little at first. Near the end she said, "I don't know why I've been hiding. Thanks for not giving up."

qa.q: How long had it been since Deepika came for Friday dinner?
qa.a: It had been six weeks.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling as Deepika's replies shrank?
qa.a: Trisha felt worried and uneasy, sensing this was not ordinary time alone but a slow fading.

qa.q: Which of Trisha's choices helped, and why?
qa.a: She reached out gently with a short, low-pressure invitation and didn't flood Deepika with worried messages, which made it easy to say yes.

qa.q: How did Deepika feel by the end of the walk?
qa.a: Deepika felt grateful and a little relieved, thanking Trisha for not giving up on her.

grounding: A friend notices someone slowly declining invitations and reaches out gently, since withdrawal grows quietly when nobody checks.

passage:
On the balcony of their Mumbai flat, Nandini, five, lay on her tummy staring at a line of ants carrying crumbs into a crack.
"Papa! Come! They're carrying food BIGGER than them!"
Naveen put down his tea and lay beside her on the floor.
"Where are they going?"
"Home, I think."
"Do they have a kitchen? Do they have a mummy? Why don't they get tired?"
"I don't know. Let's watch."
They watched. One ant dropped its crumb, and two others came to help.
Nandini gasped and grabbed Naveen's arm. "Papa! They're FRIENDS!"
He gasped too. They stayed there till the last crumb went in.

qa.q: What were the ants carrying?
qa.a: The ants were carrying crumbs into a crack.

qa.q: What was Nandini feeling when two ants came to help?
qa.a: Nandini felt amazed and delighted, gasping and grabbing Naveen's arm with wonder.

qa.q: What did Naveen do that deepened Nandini's wonder?
qa.a: He put down his tea, lay beside her and watched with her, sharing the gaze instead of simply answering her questions.

qa.q: How might Naveen have felt lying on the balcony floor?
qa.a: Naveen likely felt amused and caught up in the wonder too, gasping along with Nandini.

grounding: A child stares wide-eyed at an ant colony and asks endless questions, and a parent who shares the gaze deepens her awe.
